query: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Q235 carbon steel, a pre‐exposure microstructure with coarser grains (and hence lower grain-boundary density) will promote the formation of a more uniform and adherent protective Fe-oxide scale during high-temperature (700–900 °C) salt exposure, while a fine-grained microstructure will lead to rapid but discontinuous oxide nucleation along grain boundaries that accelerates corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 carbon steel in its as-received state, then modified by controlled pre-exposure annealing to achieve either a fine-grained or a coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform pre-exposure annealing treatments in air at two distinct temperatures (e.g., 500 °C for fine grains and 800 °C for coarse grains) to deliberately engineer different grain sizes and associated oxide‐forming microstructures before exposing the samples to a salt-laden environment.
generation.conditions: Expose all annealed samples to aggressive salt conditions at high temperature (700–900 °C) while including control experiments at room temperature, ensuring identical alloy composition and environmental parameters. Comprehensive characterization (e.g., impurity profiles, phase analysis, EBSD) will be performed to verify that differences are isolated to grain size.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain size and the associated grain-boundary density that directly influence the nucleation and growth kinetics of the oxide scale.
generation.mechanism: Coarse-grained Q235 steel, with fewer grain boundaries, facilitates slower, more uniform oxide growth leading to a continuous and adherent protective scale. In contrast, fine-grained steel provides a high density of fast-diffusing paths (grain boundaries) that promote rapid but discontinuous oxide formation, resulting in vulnerable regions where salt can penetrate and accelerate corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature salt exposures, the coarse-grained (high-temperature annealed) Q235 steel will exhibit a more homogeneous, continuous oxide scale, reduced net mass change, and slower corrosion rates compared to the fine-grained variant. At room temperature, such differences will be less pronounced due to slower kinetic processes.
generation.baseline: Q235 carbon steel with a standard, unmodified microstructure, which is expected to show intermediate oxide characteristics and moderate corrosion rates under the same conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to apply primarily under high-temperature salt-rich exposures (700–900 °C) where oxidation kinetics are rapid and grain-boundary effects are pronounced. Its applicability at lower temperatures or in environments where other factors (e.g., inclusion chemistry) dominate may be limited.
generation.uncertainty: Some uncertainty remains regarding the exclusive role of grain size independent of other secondary effects from annealing. Additional in-depth compositional and phase characterizations are needed to rule out contributions from impurities and other microstructural changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples using controlled annealing: one set annealed at ~500 °C (fine grains) and one at ~800 °C (coarse grains). Characterize the grain sizes, impurity levels, and oxide scale pre- and post-exposure using SEM/EBSD and XRD. Expose both sets to a standardized salt spray environment at 700–900 °C as well as to room temperature conditions.
measurements: Grain size and grain-boundary density via EBSD
Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and phase composition via SEM and XRD
Net mass change during salt exposure
Corrosion rate and localized damage assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coarse-grained samples do not show significantly improved oxide integrity (i.e., more continuous, adherent scales), reduced mass change, or better corrosion resistance compared to fine-grained samples under high-temperature salt conditions, or if subsequent characterization reveals that factors other than grain size dominate the behavior, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

In this study, the microstructures and mechanical properties of Al0.3CoCrFeNi HEAs after cold rolling and subsequent annealing at 800, 900, and 1000 °C were systematically investigated. The detailed conclusions were draw as follows. (1) The microstructures in 800 °C-, 900 °C-, and 1000 °C-annealed specimens showed the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening, respectively. (2) Two types of B2 phases were precipitated after cold rolling and subsequent annealing. The sizes of B2 precipitates along the grain boundaries increased but their volume fractions decreased with increasing the annealing temperature. These grain-boundary precipitates refined the grain sizes into the quasi ultra-fine grain regime (~0.9 μm) and fine grain regime (~2.2 and ~7.2 μm) in 800 °C-, 900 °C-, and 1000 °C-annealed specimens. (3) The 900 °C- and 1000 °C-annealed specimens with the recrystallized grains and B2 precipitates possessed the higher strength than the as-cast one. The precipitation strengthening contributions were calculated to occupy ~10.5% and ~9.1% of yield strengths, respectively. proposals.intervention: Systematic pre-exposure annealing to engineer distinct grain sizes and oxide‐forming microstructures
proposals.conditions: Anneal samples at two temperature regimes (e.g., 500 °C to produce a refined grain structure versus 800 °C to induce coarser grains) in air before exposing them to salt-laden atmospheres at 700–900 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain size and grain-boundary density that control oxide scale nucleation and growth
proposals.mechanism: Annealing modifies the microstructure such that coarse-grained samples form a more continuous, slower-growing protective Fe-oxide film, while fine-grained steels—with higher grain-boundary area—promote rapid oxidation but potentially discontinuous scale formation and preferential salt penetration along the boundaries
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under identical hot-corrosion conditions, coarse-grained (high-temperature annealed) Q235 steel will display enhanced oxide-scale integrity, reduced mass change, and lower corrosion rates relative to the fine-grained variant; differences should diminish at lower (room temperature) regimes where salt kinetics are minimal
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the role of microstructural features induced by annealing on high-temperature oxide scale stability and consequent corrosion protection, thereby testing a mechanistic hypothesis on the persistence or failure of protection under aggressive salt conditions

proposals.intervention: Controlled introduction and relief of residual stresses via mechanical pre-straining followed by stress-relief annealing
proposals.conditions: Prepare two sets: one subjected to controlled cold work (e.g., 10–15% plastic strain) without stress relief and another that undergoes full stress-relief annealing (e.g., 600 °C for 2 hours) prior to exposure; then expose both sets to cyclic salt spray at 700–900 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: The density of dislocations and residual stress fields at the steel surface
proposals.mechanism: Residual stresses and high dislocation densities can serve as diffusion pathways for oxygen and salt species, thereby accelerating oxide breakdown or facilitating the ingress of corrosive species. The stress-relieved sample is expected to form a more adherent and uniform oxide scale that resists corrosion
proposals.predicted_outcome: The pre-strained (non-annealed) Q235 steel will show higher mass change and more localized corrosion (micro-pitting) compared to its stress-relieved counterpart under high-temperature salt exposure, while both behave similarly under ambient conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By isolating the impact of residual stress and defect density on oxide scale formation and salt penetration, this study provides a testable hypothesis to explain why corrosion protection might fail at high temperatures despite acceptable performance at room temperature

proposals.intervention: Modulation of surface inclusions and minor element segregation by controlled deoxidation and controlled re-oxidation treatments
proposals.conditions: Prepare two batches of Q235 steel: one with standard inclusions (Mn-, Si-oxides) as received and one processed with an additional deoxidation/refining step to minimize inclusions; then subject both batches to an annealing treatment in air at ~700 °C followed by exposure in salt-laden high-temperature environments
proposals.structural_mediator: Presence and distribution of non-metallic inclusions that locally alter oxidation kinetics and oxide-scale adherence
proposals.mechanism: Minor inclusions act as local catalysts or inhibitors for oxide scale formation and may either pin the oxide or lead to initiation sites for scale spallation under salt attack. Their presence might promote a protective oxide film in some regimes or conversely lead to localized failures
proposals.predicted_outcome: The as-received Q235 steel (with inclusions) is predicted to form heterogeneous oxides with alternating protective and vulnerable zones, leading to moderate corrosion resistance at room temperature but accelerated degradation under high-temperature salt exposure, relative to the processed inclusion-minimized steel
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction tests whether intrinsic compositional inhomogeneities and inclusion-driven microstructural heterogeneity govern the transition from corrosion protection to degradation under aggressive environments, providing a clear mechanistic hypothesis

proposals.intervention: Variation of the ambient oxygen partial pressure during the pre-exposure annealing to control oxide phase composition
proposals.conditions: Anneal Q235 steel samples under two different atmospheres: (a) ambient air and (b) an oxygen-lean (argon with controlled O2 level) environment at ~800 °C for a fixed period, followed by exposure to standardized salt-spray cycles at 700–900 °C
proposals.structural_mediator: The resulting oxide phase composition and microstructure (e.g., formation of Fe3O4 versus Fe2O3 phases)
proposals.mechanism: Different oxygen availabilities during annealing lead to distinct oxide scale compositions and microstructures. A scale rich in a particular phase (e.g., Fe3O4) might be denser and more adherent, resisting aggressive salt attack better than a more porous Fe2O3-dominated scale
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed in oxygen-lean environments are expected to develop a more uniform and compact Fe3O4-rich oxide layer, exhibiting reduced mass change and improved retention of corrosion protection under high-temperature salt exposure compared to samples annealed in ambient air; these differences should be negligible at room-temperature exposures where oxide kinetics are slower
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By focusing on the oxide scale chemistry and its formation conditions, this study provides a mechanistic pathway that links the pre-exposure state (oxide chemistry influenced by annealing atmosphere) to subsequent corrosion behavior under different temperature regimes, with specific observations that could falsify the mechanism if oxide phases do not correlate with corrosion performance

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction directly targets the microstructural origin of oxide scale stability by altering grain size via controlled annealing, thereby potentially explaining why corrosion protection persists or fails under high-temperature salt exposures.
critiques.constraints: It respects material system (Q235 steel) and tests under specified temperature regimes. However, the annealing temperatures chosen (500 °C vs 800 °C) may need careful calibration to avoid altering other material properties inadvertently.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound since grain size and grain-boundary density are known to influence oxidation kinetics and oxide film continuity. The idea that coarse grains produce a more continuous protective oxide scale while fine grains lead to discontinuities is plausible.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible with established heat treatment and corrosion testing methods.
critiques.evidence: The provided literature (e.g., PMC8840145) demonstrates that annealing temperature affects grain size and precipitate distribution, which in turn influence oxidation behavior in related alloys.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that grain size might not be the only or dominant factor controlling oxide film formation; other microstructural or compositional changes during annealing could confound the results.
critiques.fix: Include comprehensive characterization (e.g., impurity profiles and phase analysis) to ensure that grain size is isolated as the governing factor rather than secondary effects from annealing.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction addresses the question by testing whether variations in surface inclusions and minor element segregation influence oxide scale formation and corrosion behavior under different temperature regimes.
critiques.constraints: It satisfies the material constraint (Q235 steel) and keeps the operational conditions intact. The processing modifications (deoxidation/re-oxidation) are acceptable but must not compromise the bulk properties of Q235.
critiques.physical_soundness: The concept that inclusions and compositional segregation affect local oxidation kinetics is physically sound; inclusions can act as local catalysts or inhibitors for oxide formation and affect scale adhesion.
critiques.feasibility: The proposed deoxidation and subsequent annealing treatments are standard metallurgical practices, making this approach feasible.
critiques.evidence: Although some evidence (e.g., PMC10254199 and PMC6908586) illustrates the influence of oxide inclusions on oxidation in other alloy systems, direct evidence in Q235 is less abundant, making the mechanistic link somewhat indirect.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk lies in the possibility that inclusions may not be the dominant factor controlling corrosion behavior in Q235; their effect might be overshadowed by other microstructural features such as grain boundaries.
critiques.fix: Integrate detailed microstructural and compositional mapping (e.g., using SEM/EDS) both before and after exposure to clearly isolate the influence of inclusions from other variables.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach tests the role of residual stresses and dislocation densities in corrosion behavior, a plausible mechanism influencing oxide scale integrity under high-temperature salt exposure.
critiques.constraints: The study is designed for Q235 steel and specifies controlled mechanical pre-straining followed by stress-relief annealing, aligning with the material and operational constraints. However, high-temperature exposures might inherently relax residual stresses, which must be accounted for.
critiques.physical_soundness: While residual stresses and dislocation densities can affect diffusion pathways and oxidation, the mechanism might be less direct for corrosion protection compared to microstructural factors like grain size or oxide composition.
critiques.feasibility: The mechanical treatments and subsequent annealing are standard processes, making the approach feasible. However, measurements of residual stress post-exposure might be challenging.
critiques.evidence: The provided references (e.g., PMC10241162 and PMC7033692) support the influence of dislocations and stress on material behavior in deformation contexts, although direct correlation with high-temperature corrosion in Q235 is not well established.
critiques.main_risk: The core risk is that residual stresses might relax during the high-temperature salt exposure, thereby diminishing the intended differences between the pre-strained and stress-relieved samples.
critiques.fix: Incorporate in-situ or post-exposure stress measurement techniques (such as X-ray diffraction residual stress analysis) to verify that the stress differences persist during the corrosion tests.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction isolates the impact of the pre-exposure oxide scale chemistry by varying the annealing atmosphere, directly linking oxide phase composition to subsequent corrosion performance under aggressive salt exposure.
critiques.constraints: It is within the confines of Q235 steel and uses controlled annealing environments to tailor oxide scales, meeting the operational constraints stated.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound because different oxygen partial pressures during annealing can lead to distinct oxide phases (e.g., Fe3O4 vs Fe2O3), which have known differences in density, adhesion, and protective properties.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is readily feasible using controlled atmosphere furnaces and standard corrosion testing procedures.
critiques.evidence: The conclusions in studies like PMC8200011 support the idea that variations in processing atmosphere influence oxide composition and subsequent corrosion behavior, which is analogous to the proposed mechanism.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is ensuring that the exact oxide phase composition, once formed, remains stable during subsequent high-temperature salt exposure so that differences can be clearly attributed to the pre-exposure annealing atmosphere.
critiques.fix: Implement real-time oxide phase monitoring (e.g., through in-situ XRD during early stages of exposure) to confirm that the distinct oxide chemistries persist under high-temperature conditions.

decision.rationale: Direction A most directly isolates a pre‐exposure microstructural factor—grain size and grain-boundary density—that can govern how a protective Fe-oxide scale forms during high-temperature salt exposure. Although annealing can lead to other changes than grain structure, this risk can be mitigated by thorough compositional and phase characterization to confirm that grain size is the dominant variable. Furthermore, the approach clearly differentiates performance at high temperature versus lower room‐temperature regimes, meeting the question’s requirements and supported by previous studies.
